title: Drennan v. Star Paving Co.
summary: Reasonable reliance on a subcontractor’s bid made it temporarily irrevocable without itself constituting acceptance of the subcontract.
notes:
Court: Supreme Court of California (1958).

Do not collapse irrevocability into acceptance. The notes’ Holman decision likewise rejects automatic acceptance merely from using and listing a subcontractor’s bid. The negligence discussion is an alternative possibility considered by the opinion, not the basis actually adjudicated.

sections.Parties: Drennan, a general contractor, sued Star Paving, the subcontractor that submitted a paving bid.
sections.Material Facts: Star quoted $7,131.60 for the Monte Vista school paving work shortly before general bids were due. Drennan used it in a $317,385 bid, named Star, and provided the required bid bond. After Drennan won, Star announced an estimating mistake and demanded at least $15,000. Drennan promptly insisted on the original bid and ultimately hired another paver for $10,848.60.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court awarded the $3,717 difference. The Supreme Court of California affirmed. The assigned introduction contrasts James Baird, and the following notes address preparations, reciprocal obligations, and the later Restatement § 87(2).
sections.Issue: Could the subcontractor revoke before communicated acceptance when it had reason to expect the general contractor to rely on its bid?
sections.Holding: The reliance supported an implied subsidiary promise not to revoke, giving the general contractor a reasonable opportunity to accept after award of the main contract. The court sustained the damages award.
sections.Reasoning: Using the bid was neither an acceptance binding both parties nor consideration for an expressly bargained-for option. Section 90 supplied a reliance-based reason to hold the offer open. The court analogized to § 45’s protection for beginning invited performance, without treating this bid as a performance-only offer. Star expected and wanted the bid used. Drennan’s commitment to the owner made withdrawal prejudicial. Known or reasonably apparent error would defeat justified reliance, while the range of bids here did not put Drennan on such notice. The general contractor could not delay to shop for a better deal or reopen bargaining and still insist on a continuing option.

priorVersions.summary: A general contractor’s reasonable reliance made the subcontractor’s bid temporarily irrevocable in the circumstances presented.
priorVersions.notes: Starter brief. Track the sequence of offer, reliance, attempted revocation, and acceptance. Add the limits concerning known error and bid shopping.

sections.Parties: General contractor Drennan sued subcontractor Star Paving.
sections.Material Facts: Drennan used Star’s paving bid in his successful general bid. Star then claimed a pricing mistake and refused to perform at the bid price; replacement performance cost more.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court awarded Drennan the additional replacement cost. The California Supreme Court affirmed.
sections.Issue: Could Star revoke after Drennan reasonably relied on the bid but before acceptance was communicated?
sections.Holding: The reliance supplied a basis for holding the offer open for a reasonable opportunity to accept.
sections.Reasoning: Star should reasonably have expected its bid to be used in the general bid. Drennan’s reliance was reasonable, and the circumstances justified protection against revocation.
